message:
I run deliveries for a small furniture restorer and I've got a few things to sort for tomorrow.

Can you suggest a name for our new delivery van (staff vote, nothing rude)?

Tomorrow the van can't leave the depot before 08:30 and must be back by 12:00. Three drops, each takes 15 minutes to unload. Drop A has a delivery window of 09:00 to 10:00. Drop B is a shop that needs its delivery done before it opens at 09:30. Drop C is an office that won't accept anything before 11:00. Driving times: depot to A 30 min, depot to B 20 min, depot to C 45 min, A to B 25 min, A to C 40 min, B to C 50 min. The driver also needs a 30-minute break somewhere before 12:00. What order should he go in, and what's the timeline?

Could you also rewrite our delivery text so it sounds friendlier than "Driver arriving. Be in."? List three things the driver should check on furniture before handing it over. Should we give customers a paper delivery note or an emailed one? And define "proof of delivery" in a line for our new part-timer. One more thing: we're thinking of texting customers the evening before with a rough arrival time. Could you draft that evening-before text too, keeping it under 160 characters so it goes as a single message?
response:
## Van name ideas

- **Chester** (as in chest of drawers)
- **Sir Veneer**
- **Dovetail Dan**
- **The Bureau Express**
- **Van Gogh**

## Tomorrow's route: B → A → C

This is the only order that works.

- **B has to come first.** Unloading there has to finish by 09:30. Going to A first means arriving at A at 09:00 at the earliest, finishing at 09:15, and reaching B at 09:40, which is too late.
- **C has to come last,** because the office won't accept anything before 11:00.

| Time | Activity |
|---|---|
| 08:30 | Leave depot |
| 08:50 | Arrive at B (20 min) |
| 08:50–09:05 | Unload at B ✓ done before 09:30 |
| 09:30 | Arrive at A (25 min) |
| 09:30–09:45 | Unload at A ✓ within 09:00–10:00 |
| 10:25 | Arrive at C (40 min) |
| 10:25–10:55 | **30-minute break** (he'd be waiting anyway) |
| 11:00–11:15 | Unload at C ✓ not before 11:00 |
| 12:00 | Back at depot (45 min) ✓ |

**There is no slack at the end of the day.** The run finishes at exactly 12:00. Once he unloads at C at 11:00 at the earliest, 15 minutes of unloading plus 45 minutes of driving brings him back at 12:00 no matter what. If the office keeps him waiting, or traffic is bad on the way back, he'll be late. To get some margin, it's worth asking:

- **Can C accept at 10:45?** That alone would give 15 minutes of slack.
- **Is 12:00 a hard deadline?** If so, the driver and the office should both know it's tight.

The morning has some slack: about 25 minutes at B and 15 at A.

## Friendlier arrival text

> Hi [Name], your driver is on the way and should be with you in about [X] minutes. See you soon!

## Three things to check before handing over furniture

1. **Condition:** check for new scratches, dents or marks from the journey, compared with how it left the workshop.
2. **Function:** open and close drawers and doors, and check handles, hinges and castors work.
3. **Completeness and placement:** make sure all parts, keys and fittings are there, and that the piece stands level and stable where the customer wants it.

Taking a quick photo after placement helps if there's a dispute later.

## Paper or emailed delivery note?

**Use an emailed one, signed on a phone or tablet at the door.** It gives you a timestamped record that can't be lost, and the customer gets a copy automatically. Keep a few paper notes in the van for customers without email, or for when the signal drops.

## Proof of delivery, for the part-timer

> **Proof of delivery** is the customer's signature (and ideally a photo) confirming they received the item, in good condition, at a specific date and time.

## Evening-before text

> Hi [Name], your furniture from [Company] is due tomorrow between [time] and [time]. Reply if that doesn't suit. Thanks!

With real details filled in, for example "Hi Sarah… Oak & Ash Restoration… 9:00 and 10:00", it comes to about 125 characters, so it fits in one message unless the company name is very long.

**Use a straight apostrophe (') in "doesn't", not a curly one (’).** Some phones and texting tools insert curly apostrophes automatically. A curly apostrophe switches the message to a different encoding with a 70-character limit, so it would be split into two texts.
